newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan faults FASB derivatives accounting rules.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan faults FASB derivatives accounting rules.

text.p: The Financial Accounting Standards Boards' latest derivatives accounting proposals have now come under the fire of Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan.
Not only did Greenspan tell the accounting board to slow down and allow more time for industry input, he recommended the board consider a different proposal altogether.

"While we support FASB's objective of promoting greater transparency of derivatives in financial statements, the proposal continues to take a piecemeal approach to fair value accounting, which raises a number of concerns," Greenspan wrote in a July 31 letter to the independent board, the panel that designs the accounting rules companies must abide by.
Greenspan recommended to the board an alternative plan, which would call for expanded disclosures without dramatically changing current accounting practices.

His comments come after a group of top executives from major U.S. companies blasted FASB for moving quickly to finalize the rules, which the group said would have an impact on the capital markets and could weaken a conmpany's ability to manage risk.
The board quickly responded to those concerns, defending the rules and maintaining its stance that the rules would likely be finalized by year-end.

"Companies currently omit from their financial statements bilions of dollars of transactions in derivatives instruments each year," FASB Chairman Edmund L. Jenkins told the corporate executives and others.
"That makes it difficult for investors to properly evaluate those companies' financial position and risks."
In July, the accounting board opted to move ahead with a final rule on the accounting for derivatives used in hedging, even against the wishes of key market players and some top lawmakers.
The rules require that all derivatives be recognized in the financial statement. Gains and losses resulting from changes in fair values would be accounted for depending on the use of the derivatives.
The accounting board has been pressured by Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt to finish the project, which has been in progress for several years now.

But in the four-page letter, Greenspan outlined many problems with the rules, noting that institutions using derivatives to offset their risks would have to make "significant systems changes" while those who didn't have hedged positions would not have such burdens.
"The proposal may discourage prudent risk management activities and in some cases could present misleading financial information," Greenspan said.
